newsitem.title: USA: George Wallace 'the movie' stirs anger in Alabama.
newsitem.headline: George Wallace 'the movie' stirs anger in Alabama.

text.p: A new made-for-TV movie about former Gov. George Wallace has some folks in Alabama hopping mad over its fictional portrayal of the one-time segregationist as a hapless figure bent on suicide.

The $12 million Turner Network Television production, which stars Gary Sinise as Wallace, began filming last week. But its producers have opted for a movie-set in California after being all but banished from Alabama.
"We kept the Yankees at the border. Rally round the flag, boys!" quipped Wallace spokesman David Azbell. "That's one victory. Let's see if we can win another."

After reviewing the film's script, members of the Wallace family were so enraged that they filled up a four-page memo with alleged historical inaccuracies and distortions and forwarded it to executives at TNT, part of Ted Turner's Atlanta-based media empire.
They have since hired a lawyer, threatened to file a lawsuit and have even sought the advice of Henry Kissinger, who sued TNT in a similar dispute.

Last week, their cause also got some powerful political support from the current Alabama governor, Republican Fob James, who denounced the filmmakers as "scoundrels" and singled out the screenwriter as a "revolting, damnable liar."

"To portray (Wallace) as an illiterate, ignorant, corn-pone Hee Haw character is not only an insult to him, it's an insult to all the people of Alabama," fumed the former governor's son, George Wallace Jr.

Wallace, who was first elected governor of Alabama in 1962, drew national attention by proclaiming "segregation forever" during his inaugural address. But it was his televised stand in "the schoolhouse door" against integration at the University of Alabama that immortalised him as a nefarious icon of the Civil Rights era.

The now-ailing politician, paralysed from the waist down by an assassination attempt during his 1972 presidential campaign, later renounced segregation and has struggled over the past quarter-century to redeem his image by championing the cause of racial reconciliation.
George Wallace Jr. complains that the three-hour TNT movie, scheduled to air in August, spends an inordinate amount of time on the bodily functions of his paraplegic father.
But the family's main bone of contention are two episodes that depict incidents which they say never happened.

One presents a fictional Wallace aide who considers killing the former governor with an ice pick. Later, the same character helps to stop a paralysed Wallace from ending his life by pitching his wheelchair off the porch of another real-life former Alabama governor, "Big Jim" Folsom.

"There's no need to create the fiction of an attempted suicide on the part of my dad or an alleged attempted murder of my dad by an orderly at the governor's mansion, or portraying my mother in such a way that she was not," said Wallace Jr.

Moviemakers concede that some scenes depict events that never actually took place. But they say the film's intent is to go beyond Wallace in order to illustrate his era. And they have assembled a Hollywood staff with some formidable credentials to achieve that objective.

"I'm not doing a documentary about George Wallace any more than Shakespeare was doing a documentary about Richard III," said the film's Emmy-award-winning director, John Frankenheimer, who's past films include "The Manchurian Candidate" and "The Birdman of Alcatraz."
"The basic premise of the movie is factual. We've researched this subject for years," he added.

State officials have not been moved by that argument, however. The Alabama Film Office, set up to encourage Hollywood production companies to shoot films in the state, told TNT last week that it could provide no help for a Wallace production in Alabama.
The Wallace Foundation, a non-profit historical group, also has cut off assistance to the project.
Still, the TNT film staff appear to have accepted their exile with philosophic resignation and a wry sense of history.

"You come into anybody's neighbourhood, you don't want to come in like Sherman into Georgia," said producer Mark Carliner, referring to the famous Union general who burned Atlanta during the Civil War.
